clue.text: Countryside walkers go on grass regularly (8)

blocks.note: to go on — to talk at length — is to ramble
the even letters of gRaSs, taken 'regularly'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures hikers misbehaving on the lawn, but 'go on' means chatter — the chatty sense of RAMBLE — before grass surrenders its alternate letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramblers are Britain's recreational countryside walkers — the Ramblers is the national walking charity — so the definition is close to literal, plural matching plural.

clue.text: Principles of Ancient Greece overthrown in the past (3)

blocks.note: the first letters of the three words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Principles' puns on 'principal': take the principal — first — letters. The toppled civilisation is pure surface drama.
explanation.definitionFit: Ago places an event in the past, as in 'long ago' — an adverb matching the clue's adverbial phrase.

blocks.note: to shove gracelessly through a space, as when pushing past someone in a hurry
a flat-bottomed vessel used on canals and rivers for heavy cargo

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has you rowing badly; the split comes at 'in', leaving a verb on one side and a noun on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: To barge is to blunder or shove your way somewhere, and a barge is the flat-bottomed cargo boat — one spelling doing two unrelated jobs.

clue.text: Celtic and Real played with a kind of energy (10)

definitions.note: ELECTRICAL is an adjective while 'a kind of energy' reads as a noun phrase; the setter lets the adjective stand for electrical energy itself, a common liberty with kinds and types.

blocks.note: two famous football clubs supply the ten letters — 'and' adds none

explanation.walkthrough: Celtic and Real Madrid keep the surface on the pitch, where 'played' looks innocent — but it is the anagram indicator rearranging the clubs' letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Electrical names the energy carried by electric charge — mains power — one of the standard kinds of energy in physics.

blocks.note: to formally support or back a proposal put to a meeting
a mo is short for a moment — a very brief unit of time

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as 'I'll be right back', which is the misdirection: split it at 'in' and each half defines the answer on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: To second a motion is to back it, and a mo — a moment — is a second: a verb on one side, a noun on the other.

clue.text: Physical training on esplanade is timely (6)

blocks.note: the seaside promenade — an esplanade
PT is the standard abbreviation for physical training

explanation.walkthrough: In an across entry 'on' means 'following', so the piece the clue names first ends up second in the answer. That reversal is a positional convention worth learning, and it points the other way in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Prompt means acting without delay — a prompt reply is a timely one — adjective for adjective.

blocks.note: to peer is to look closely

explanation.walkthrough: Say 'peer' aloud and you hear the answer — a classic seaside soundalike pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A pier is a structure built out into the sea that shelters the water behind it, which is why dictionaries define it partly as a breakwater.

clue.text: Gold box right next to a group of musicians (9)

blocks.note: OR is heraldry's word for gold — a crossword staple
a chest is a box
R abbreviates right
the little word counts itself into the answer

explanation.walkthrough: Even the 'a' is a working part here, gluing itself onto the end — not every small word is padding.
explanation.definitionFit: An orchestra is a large ensemble of musicians — strings, wind and percussion playing together — the everyday sense of the word.

clue.text: Acquisition of professional remedy meant amateur excluded (11)

blocks.note: a pro is a professional
a cure is a remedy
MEANT once its A has gone
A for amateur, the sports abbreviation — this is the letter 'excluded' from MEANT

explanation.walkthrough: Amateur = A comes from sport, where A once distinguished unpaid players from professionals — apt in a clue that opens with PRO.
explanation.definitionFit: Procurement is the formal business word for acquiring goods and services — an organisation's procurement is its acquisition — noun matching noun.

blocks.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flexible' bends COURSE into shape — a neat pairing, since a river's course begins at its source.
explanation.definitionFit: A source is where something originates — a river's source, the source of a rumour — a plain synonym for origin.

blocks.note: the Roman orator plus the exclamation supply the eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Translation' is a sly indicator for a Latin orator: it rearranges Cicero's letters, NO included, rather than his prose.
explanation.definitionFit: Coercion is compelling someone by pressure or threats, which is exactly what using force on them amounts to — both nouns.

blocks.note: seven letters sent 'travelling'
the compass abbreviation, tacked on unshuffled

explanation.walkthrough: The setter splits the work: an anagram builds the front while NE simply follows it — the compass point stays out of the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Limestone is a sedimentary rock — the stone of the Pennines and of cave country — so 'rock' defines it by its category.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'Improvised' — just what a trio might do on stage — is the anagram signal, and the musical surface hides a much drier word.
explanation.definitionFit: An interaction is parties acting on each other — its Latin roots are 'between' and 'action' — so a joint performance is what the word literally describes.

blocks.note: hidden across the two words: seVEN UShers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Surrounding' says the ushers have the goddess inside them — the answer runs straight across the gap between the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus is the Roman goddess of love and beauty — a definition by example, since 'goddess' could name many others.

clue.text: Badly parse a term for boundaries (10)

blocks.note: the ten letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: A self-aware clue — parsing it is exactly what you are doing — with 'badly' handling the mangling.
explanation.definitionFit: Strictly parameters are variables, but everyday use — 'within the parameters' — means limits or boundaries, and that looser sense is the one defined here.

clue.text: Very sad ending to Hamlet leads to riots against Gertrude in consequence (6)

blocks.note: the play's final letter — its 'ending'
the leading letters of the five words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads to' looks like joinery but is the instruction: take the leads — the front letters — of the last five words. Fitting, for a play that ends strewn with bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragic means very sad — desperately so — and the word comes straight from tragedy, the genre Hamlet defines.

clue.text: Astronauts initially strap up a complicated piece of equipment (9)

blocks.note: 'initially' keeps just its first letter
eight more letters for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' trims Astronauts to a single A before 'complicated' shuffles everything — the spacewalk surface disguises a very general word.
explanation.definitionFit: Apparatus is the equipment assembled for a particular purpose — gym apparatus, laboratory apparatus — so the definition names its everyday sense.

blocks.note: hidden across all three words: pariS ART REvolution

explanation.walkthrough: Sartre was the great philosopher of Paris cafe society, and he is literally sitting in 'Paris art revolution'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Paul Sartre, the French existentialist, is a philosopher defined by example — and the Parisian surface is a broad hint at which one.

clue.text: Withdraw from drive back across Australia (6)

blocks.note: to drive back an attack is to repel it — it opens around the A
the one-letter abbreviation, as in A$ for the Australian dollar

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive back' is one unit meaning REPEL, not a reversal — the surface wants you picturing an outback road trip that never happens.
explanation.definitionFit: To repeal a law is to withdraw it — take it back off the statute book — both verbs in their base form.

clue.text: Dish overwhelms a sense of taste (6)

blocks.note: a plate is a dish — it swallows the A
the letter taken inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Overwhelms' is the container signal: the dish engulfs the A, and the food surface steers you neatly past the anatomical answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The palate is the roof of the mouth and, by extension, the faculty of tasting itself — a discerning palate — so the definition names that extended use.

blocks.note: cooked in hot fat — it wraps round the N
N is the abbreviation for noon, as on old timetables

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' looks like an anagram indicator but is fodder here: FRIED, with midday's N dropped in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mate is the informal British word for a friend — a pal — rather than the chess move or the ship's officer.

blocks.note: hidden across the two words: oSCAR Frequently

explanation.walkthrough: Oscar clutches the answer literally: it runs from inside his name into the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffler is an older word for a scarf — something wound round the neck to muffle you against the cold — not the car silencer.

clue.text: Incentives to buy liberal Guardian at first, then Independent, FT and Sun (4,5)

blocks.note: liberal means free — generous, unrestricted
its first letter
its first letter
already initials, so it goes in whole
its first letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' serves every paper in the queue — the FT being initials already — and a Guardian puzzle clueing its rivals is a nice in-joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Free gifts are the giveaways papers bundle to tempt readers, so they are incentives to buy — a plural phrase matching a plural definition.

clue.text: Current business account’s opening in island (5)

blocks.note: I is the physics symbol for electric current
the showbiz-style shortening
its opening letter

explanation.walkthrough: Three abbreviations in a row — physics, slang and an initial — assemble the Balearic party island out of office paperwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic islands, so 'island' defines it by example — the financial surface hides a holiday destination.

clue.text: Member of clergy loses hat immediately according to Shakespeare (4)

blocks.note: a canon is a cathedral cleric — about to lose its top

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the 'hat' is the top letter, so the C comes off CANON. 'I come, anon!' is how Shakespeare's characters say they'll be right there.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is the archaic adverb for soon or immediately, familiar from Shakespeare — hence the qualifier steering you towards Elizabethan English.

blocks.note: 1st — 'first' written with figures, the 1 reading as I
a tango is a dance — the question mark flags the definition by example

explanation.walkthrough: Writing 'first' as 1st and then reading the figure 1 as the letter I is the leap here. The question mark concedes that a tango is only one dance among many.
explanation.definitionFit: Distance is reserve in the emotional sense — keeping someone at a distance is treating them with cool detachment — both nouns.

blocks.note: illicit means unlawful

explanation.walkthrough: ILLICIT and ELICIT are not quite identical aloud, and the setter admits it: 'roughly' licenses the loose soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: To elicit a reaction is to produce or draw it out — both verbs — and the pair here is a famous confusable in written English.

blocks.note: tablets are pills — unwrapping strips off the outer P and S

explanation.walkthrough: 'Unwrap' means exactly what it says: peel the outside letters off PILLS, the way you would the packaging.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill means unwell — the plainest of synonyms — and the medicinal surface keeps both words in the sickroom.

blocks.note: university, informally — the academic place
a son is one kind of offspring — the question mark allows for daughters

explanation.walkthrough: An 'academic offspring' sounds like a professor's child; the wordplay just glues UNI to SON.
explanation.definitionFit: To act or speak in unison is to do it in complete agreement — the word literally means 'one sound'.

blocks.note: not big = small
do-it-yourself — it wraps around SMALL

explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Sadly' is the misdirection: it makes the definition read as a passing aside rather than the word being defined. Home-improvement for DIY is a standard dodge.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismally means in a gloomy, cheerless way — to fail dismally is to fail sadly — adverb for adverb.
